name: MyHTML
baseline: gumbo and html5ever (Rust, via html2html_lib C binding)
workload: Parsing real-world website homepages (e.g. 163.com, 1688.com, 360.com, ~100-500 sampled sites) with myhtml (threaded and single-threaded), Google gumbo, and a Rust html5ever C binding; per-page wall-clock parse time recorded in CSV.
claimed_speedup: Example row (163.com): gumbo 0.05153s, html5ever 0.03694s, myhtml 0.00529s, myhtml_single 0.00845s -> myhtml ~7-10x faster than gumbo and ~7x faster than html5ever on that page (derived from page data); pattern of myhtml being several times faster than both repeats across most sampled rows.
stars_or_usage: 1.7k stars; multiple language bindings (Perl, Crystal, Elixir, Swift)
tradeoffs: Only builds an HTML5 tree (no CSS selector engine); threaded async parsing adds API complexity; project author now directs users to the successor lexbor project (already catalogued) for new work.
caveats: Benchmark repo (by the same author, not independent) states no compiler flags or CPU model, so capped at tier C despite being a real reproducible corpus benchmark with public code; benchmark repo itself last pushed 2016 and myhtml's own last commit is Jan 2025; ratios shown are single-row examples from the CSV, not stated averages.
found_via: Hacker News: 'MyHTML: Fast C/C++ HTML 5 Parser Using Threads' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=12087220

name: selectolax
workload: Extract title, links, scripts, and a meta tag from the homepages of the top 754 domains (examples/benchmark.py); total wall-clock time summed over the corpus.
claimed_speedup: BeautifulSoup(html.parser) 61.02s; lxml/BeautifulSoup(lxml) 9.09s; html5_parser 16.10s; selectolax(Modest) 2.94s; selectolax(Lexbor) 2.39s -> selectolax(Lexbor) ~3.8x faster than lxml-based BeautifulSoup (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 1.68k stars; widely used in Python web-scraping stacks
tradeoffs: Python/Cython call overhead remains vs raw C; default Modest backend engine is itself unmaintained (project now recommends the Lexbor backend); benchmark task is light DOM extraction, not full traversal or mutation.
caveats: No CPU model or compiler flags stated for the compiled extension; numbers are a single wall-clock run over an unpublished, non-reproducible one-time crawl of 754 domains, not averaged trials.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: Python bindings to Modest engine (fast HTML parser with CSS selectors)' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=15820705

name: html5-parser
workload: Parsing a ~5.7MB real-world HTML document into a tree; 100 iterations for html5-parser vs 10 iterations for competing libraries, on the author's own machine with Python 3.
claimed_speedup: 35x faster than html5lib (lxml tree, HTML5 support); 8x faster than BeautifulSoup+html5lib; 2x faster than BeautifulSoup+lxml; author states an overall ~37x speedup on his system.
stars_or_usage: 706 stars; used inside the calibre e-book application
tradeoffs: Uses gumbo internally then rebuilds a libxml2-compatible tree, so it needs a compiled C extension; not a pure drop-in for lxml's own HTML parser API.
caveats: The only figure directly relevant to libxml2 is the 2x margin over BeautifulSoup+lxml; the larger 35x/37x numbers are against pure-Python html5lib, a much weaker baseline; no CPU, OS, or compiler flags stated, single ad hoc trial.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: Fast C-based HTML 5 parsing for Python' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=14588333

name: stb_xml
workload: Parsing synthetic small (72B), medium (~1KB) and large (~1MB, 10000-tag) generated XML files, timed over 10 to 100000 iterations; stb_xml's tokenizer (test_stb_xml.c) vs libxml2's xmlReadMemory (test_libxml.c).
claimed_speedup: 1MB file: stb_xml 8707 MB/s vs libxml2 46 MB/s ~ 189x faster (derived from page data); small 72B file: 188 MB/s vs 15 MB/s ~ 12.5x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O2 -std=c99 for stb_xml; gcc -lxml2 -O2 for libxml2 comparison
tradeoffs: stb_xml is a bare zero-allocation tokenizer emitting 6-byte tokens, not a validating parser or DOM builder: no namespaces, no DTD/entity handling, minimal error checking, so it does far less work per byte than libxml2's full tree build.
caveats: Claimed ratio exceeds 50x with no CPU model stated, and the two sides do materially different amounts of work (tokenize-only vs full validated DOM), so this is capped at tier C and confidence is kept low; entire repo is 2 commits made on the same day.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: Stb_XML - A 6KB XML parser that's 193x faster than libxml2' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46497825

name: MarkupEver
workload: Parse, CSS-select, and serialize a test HTML document; average microseconds per operation measured for BeautifulSoup(html.parser), BeautifulSoup(lxml), Parsel, html5lib, and MarkupEver.
claimed_speedup: Parsing: 4,927us vs BeautifulSoup(lxml) 22,809us ~ 4.6x faster (derived from page data); CSS selection: 310us vs 2,995us ~ 9.6x faster (derived from page data); Serializing: 1,952us vs 14,900us ~ 7.6x faster (derived from page data).
hardware: Manjaro Linux x86_64, 8GB RAM, Intel Core i3-1115G4
tradeoffs: Built on html5ever + servo's selectors crate internally, so the measured gap is Rust-native-code vs Python-wrapped-libxml2, not a new parsing algorithm; requires a compiled Rust extension for Python users.
caveats: Single test document only, no size/complexity given; only the project's own numbers, not independently reproduced; Rust build optimisation flags not stated even though CPU model is.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN: MarkupEver - A fast, flexible HTML/XML parser that beats BeautifulSoup' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43746250
